notes.definition: Higher tier: hormones can be used to treat infertility. A fertility drug containing FSH and LH can stimulate ovulation, and in IVF the same hormones are used to make several eggs mature so they can be collected and fertilised in a laboratory.
explanation: Some women cannot become pregnant because their levels of FSH are too low, so eggs do not mature and are not released. These women can be given FSH and LH in a 'fertility drug'. FSH causes eggs to mature in the ovary and LH stimulates their release (ovulation). The egg can then be fertilised naturally in the oviduct.

If this does not work, or if there is another problem such as blocked oviducts, the couple may be offered in vitro fertilisation (IVF). 'In vitro' means 'in glass', because fertilisation happens in the laboratory. First, the mother is given FSH and LH to stimulate the maturation of several eggs. The eggs are then collected from the mother.

The eggs are fertilised by sperm from the father in the laboratory. The fertilised eggs develop into embryos. At the stage when they are tiny balls of cells, one or two embryos are inserted into the mother's uterus (womb). If an embryo implants in the uterus lining, the woman becomes pregnant. Developments in microscopy techniques have enabled IVF treatments to develop, because eggs, sperm and early embryos must be handled and checked under a microscope.

Fertility treatment gives a woman the chance to have a baby of her own, but there are drawbacks. It is very emotionally and physically stressful: daily injections, egg collection procedures and repeated failures are hard for couples. The success rates are not high, and they fall as the woman gets older. Treatment is also expensive and may need to be repeated several times.

Fertility treatment can lead to multiple births, because a fertility drug can cause several eggs to be released, and in IVF more than one embryo may be inserted. Multiple births are a risk to both the babies and the mother: babies are more likely to be born early and with a low birth weight, and the mother faces more complications during pregnancy. For this reason doctors now usually insert only one or two embryos.

When evaluating treatments, consider the views of both patients and doctors. Patients weigh the chance of a child against the stress, cost and risks. Doctors must consider success rates, the health of mother and babies, and ethical issues, such as what happens to unused embryos, which some people believe should not be destroyed.

keyTerms.definition: Being unable to conceive a child after trying for a long time.
A drug containing FSH and LH given to stimulate egg maturation and ovulation.
Fertilisation of eggs by sperm outside the body in a laboratory, followed by insertion of embryos into the uterus.
In IVF, the tiny ball of cells formed when a fertilised egg divides.
The birth of two or more babies from one pregnancy, e.g. twins or triplets.
When an embryo attaches into the lining of the uterus, starting a pregnancy.

workedExamples.title: Calculating a success rate
workedExamples.question: A clinic carried out 240 IVF cycles in a year. 60 resulted in a live birth. Calculate the percentage success rate.
steps: Success rate = (number of live births ÷ number of cycles) × 100
workedExamples.answer: 25 %. So three in four cycles did not lead to a baby, which shows why IVF can be so stressful.

workedExamples.title: Percentage decrease with age
workedExamples.question: Using the bar chart, calculate the percentage decrease in success rate between women under 35 (32 per 100 cycles) and women aged 40 to 42 (11 per 100 cycles).

workedExamples.title: Explaining a step of IVF
workedExamples.question: Explain why a woman is given FSH and LH at the start of IVF.
steps: FSH causes eggs to mature in the ovaries.
Giving extra FSH (with LH) makes several eggs mature at once, rather than one.
More eggs can be collected, so more can be fertilised.
More embryos are available, increasing the chance of a successful pregnancy.
workedExamples.answer: To stimulate the maturation of several eggs so that more can be collected and fertilised.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think the embryo is grown in the laboratory until it is a baby.
misconceptions.right: In fact embryos are inserted into the mother's uterus when they are tiny balls of cells, only a few days old.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think IVF always works.
misconceptions.right: In fact success rates are not high, often well under one in three cycles, and they fall with age.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think fertility drugs contain oestrogen and progesterone.
misconceptions.right: In fact fertility drugs contain FSH and LH. Oestrogen and progesterone are used in contraceptives because they inhibit FSH.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think inserting many embryos is best because it raises the chance of pregnancy.
misconceptions.right: In fact it greatly raises the chance of multiple births, which are a risk to both the babies and the mother, so only one or two are inserted.

realWorld: Over a million babies worldwide have been born through IVF since the first IVF baby, Louise Brown, was born in the UK in 1978.
In the UK, the number of embryos transferred is regulated, and clinics encourage single embryo transfer to reduce twin and triplet pregnancies.
Spare embryos from IVF can be frozen for later use, donated, or destroyed, which raises ethical debate.
higherTier: Women with a low level of FSH can be given FSH and LH in a fertility drug to stimulate ovulation.
IVF involves giving a mother FSH and LH to stimulate the maturation of several eggs, which are collected and fertilised by sperm from the father in the laboratory.
The fertilised eggs develop into embryos; at the stage when they are tiny balls of cells, one or two embryos are inserted into the mother's uterus.
Fertility treatment is emotionally and physically stressful, success rates are not high, and it can lead to multiple births, which are a risk to both the babies and the mother.
Explain the use of hormones in modern reproductive technologies to treat infertility, and evaluate treatments from the perspective of patients and doctors.
examTips: Learn the IVF steps in order: FSH and LH given, eggs collected, fertilised in lab, embryos develop, one or two inserted into uterus.
Say 'stimulates the maturation of SEVERAL eggs' for IVF hormone treatment. 'To release an egg' is not enough.
The specification lists three drawbacks: emotionally and physically stressful, success rates not high, risk of multiple births. Learn all three.
For 'evaluate', give both sides (a chance of a baby of their own versus the drawbacks) and a conclusion.
Do not confuse fertility drugs (FSH and LH) with contraceptive hormones (oestrogen and progesterone).
summary: Low FSH can cause infertility; a fertility drug of FSH and LH stimulates ovulation.
IVF uses FSH and LH to make several eggs mature.
Eggs are collected and fertilised by sperm in the laboratory.
Embryos (tiny balls of cells) are inserted into the uterus, one or two at a time.
Treatment is stressful, has low success rates and risks multiple births.

questions.question: Which hormones does a 'fertility drug' contain to stimulate ovulation?
markScheme: 1 mark: FSH and LH
questions.explanation: FSH matures an egg and LH stimulates its release. Oestrogen and progesterone inhibit FSH, which is how many contraceptives work.

questions.question: A woman cannot become pregnant because eggs in her ovaries do not mature. Her body is most likely to produce too little of which hormone?
markScheme: 1 mark: FSH
questions.explanation: FSH causes eggs to mature. With low FSH, no egg matures, so none can be released or fertilised.

questions.question: In IVF, where does fertilisation take place?
markScheme: 1 mark: In a laboratory
questions.explanation: In vitro means 'in glass': eggs and sperm are mixed in the laboratory. In natural conception fertilisation happens in the oviduct.

questions.question: What does IVF stand for?
markScheme: 1 mark: In vitro fertilisation
questions.explanation: In vitro means outside the body, in the laboratory. In vivo would mean inside the living body, which is the opposite.

questions.question: Why is a woman given FSH and LH at the start of IVF treatment?
options: To build up the uterus lining
To stimulate the maturation of several eggs
To prevent the embryo being rejected
markScheme: 1 mark: To stimulate the maturation of several eggs
questions.explanation: More mature eggs means more can be collected and fertilised, giving more embryos and a better chance of success.

questions.question: At what stage are embryos inserted into the mother's uterus in IVF?
options: When they are tiny balls of cells
markScheme: 1 mark: When they are tiny balls of cells
questions.explanation: Embryos are inserted after only a few days, when they are tiny balls of cells. They then need to implant in the uterus lining.

questions.question: Why do doctors usually insert only one or two embryos during IVF?
options: To reduce the risk of multiple births
Because only one egg can be collected
Because the uterus can only hold one embryo
To increase the chance of twins
markScheme: 1 mark: To reduce the risk of multiple births
questions.explanation: Multiple births are a risk to both the babies and the mother. Several eggs are usually collected, and a uterus can hold more than one embryo, which is why the number is limited.

questions.question: Fertility treatment can lead to multiple births. Why is this a concern?
options: Multiple births always lead to genetic disorders
Multiple births are a risk to both the babies and the mother
markScheme: 1 mark: Multiple births are a risk to both the babies and the mother
questions.explanation: Babies from multiple births are more likely to be premature and have a low birth weight, and the mother is at higher risk of complications. They do not always cause genetic disorders.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT a disadvantage of IVF treatment?
options: The success rates are not high
It is emotionally and physically stressful
It gives a woman the chance to have a baby of her own
It can lead to multiple births
markScheme: 1 mark: It gives a woman the chance to have a baby of her own
questions.explanation: This is the main benefit of fertility treatment. The other three are the drawbacks named in the specification.

questions.question: Which scientific development has enabled IVF treatments to develop?
markScheme: 1 mark: Developments in microscopy techniques
questions.explanation: Eggs, sperm and early embryos are microscopic, so they must be handled and checked under a microscope during IVF.

questions.question: A woman has blocked oviducts but normal hormone levels. Which treatment is most likely to help her become pregnant?
options: A fertility drug containing FSH and LH only
markScheme: 1 mark: IVF
questions.explanation: With blocked oviducts, sperm cannot reach an egg, so making her ovulate with a fertility drug would not help. IVF bypasses the oviducts by fertilising eggs in the laboratory and placing embryos directly in the uterus.

questions.question: Why can a fertility drug containing FSH and LH lead to twins or triplets?
options: Several eggs may mature and be released at the same time
FSH causes one embryo to split into several
The hormones double the number of chromosomes
markScheme: 1 mark: Several eggs may mature and be released at the same time
questions.explanation: Extra FSH can cause more than one egg to mature, and LH triggers their release. Each can be fertilised by a different sperm, giving non-identical twins or triplets.

questions.question: Name the two hormones given in a fertility drug, and the gland that normally produces them.
markScheme: 1 mark: FSH and LH
1 mark: pituitary gland
questions.explanation: In a natural cycle the pituitary releases FSH and LH. A fertility drug supplies them when the woman's own levels are too low.

questions.question: In IVF, state what happens to the eggs after they have been collected from the mother.
markScheme: 1 mark: they are fertilised by sperm from the father in the laboratory
questions.explanation: Fertilisation in the laboratory is the 'in vitro' part of IVF.

questions.question: A woman has a low level of FSH. Explain how a fertility drug containing FSH and LH could help her to become pregnant.
markScheme: 1 mark: FSH causes an egg to mature (in the ovary)
1 mark: LH stimulates the release of the egg / ovulation, so it can be fertilised
questions.explanation: Both steps are needed: maturation (FSH) then release (LH). Once released, the egg can be fertilised naturally in the oviduct.

questions.question: Give three disadvantages of fertility treatment for the woman being treated.
markScheme: 1 mark each, any three: emotionally stressful; physically stressful (injections, egg collection); success rates are not high / may need several attempts; can lead to multiple births, which are a risk to mother and babies; expensive
questions.explanation: The specification names stress, low success rates and multiple births. Cost is also a valid point.

questions.question: Explain why it is useful to collect several eggs during IVF rather than one.
markScheme: 1 mark: not all eggs will be fertilised / not all embryos will develop or implant
1 mark: so collecting several increases the chance of a successful pregnancy (spare embryos can be frozen)
questions.explanation: Each step of IVF has a failure rate, so starting with more eggs gives more chances of at least one healthy embryo.

questions.question: Before inserting embryos into the uterus, doctors examine them under a microscope. Suggest why.
markScheme: 1 mark: to check the embryos are developing normally / cells are dividing
1 mark: so the healthiest embryo(s) can be chosen, increasing the chance of success
questions.explanation: Microscopy allows doctors to select embryos most likely to implant and develop, which links to the role of microscopy in IVF.

questions.question: IVF success rates are lower in older women. Suggest one reason why.
markScheme: 1 mark: older women have fewer eggs / their eggs are of lower quality / fewer eggs mature in response to FSH
1 mark: so fewer healthy embryos are produced or embryos are less likely to implant
questions.explanation: This is a 'suggest' question, so any sensible biological reason linked to eggs or implantation is credited.

questions.question: IVF often produces more embryos than are inserted into the uterus. Suggest ethical issues this raises.
markScheme: 1 mark: unused embryos may be destroyed
1 mark: some people believe an embryo has a right to life / is a potential human
1 mark: embryos may be frozen or used for research, which some people object to (e.g. for religious reasons)
questions.explanation: Ethical questions have no single right answer. Credit is given for clearly stated issues and different points of view.

questions.question: A clinic carried out 240 IVF cycles. 60 of them resulted in a live birth. Calculate the percentage success rate.
markScheme: 1 mark: = 25 %
questions.explanation: 60 ÷ 240 = 0.25. Multiply by 100 to get 25 %. So 75 % of cycles did not produce a baby.

questions.question: The success rate of IVF for women under 35 is 32 live births per 100 cycles. Calculate the number of live births expected from 150 cycles.
markScheme: 1 mark: = 48

questions.question: An IVF cycle costs £5200, plus £1300 for the fertility drugs. A couple pays for three cycles. Calculate the total cost.
markScheme: 1 mark: 5200 + 1300 = £6500 per cycle
questions.explanation: Add the costs for one cycle first, then multiply by the number of cycles. Cost is one of the reasons treatment is stressful.

questions.question: Of 400 births following IVF at one clinic, 64 were multiple births (twins or triplets). Calculate the percentage of births that were multiple births.
markScheme: 1 mark: = 16 %
questions.explanation: 64 ÷ 400 = 0.16, which is 16 %. This is much higher than for natural conception, which is why fewer embryos are now inserted.

questions.question: The IVF success rate is 32 per 100 cycles for women under 35 and 11 per 100 cycles for women aged 40 to 42. Calculate the percentage decrease in success rate. Give your answer to 3 significant figures.
markScheme: 1 mark: decrease = 32 − 11 = 21
questions.explanation: Percentage decrease uses the original value (32) as the denominator. Dividing by 11 instead gives 191 %, which is wrong. The simple difference, 21, is in percentage points, not a percentage decrease.

questions.question: Explain why fertility treatment can lead to multiple births, and why this is a concern.
markScheme: Indicative content: fertility drugs contain FSH (and LH); FSH can cause several eggs to mature; LH causes them to be released; each egg can be fertilised; in IVF more than one embryo may be inserted into the uterus; more than one may implant; multiple births are a risk to both the babies and the mother; babies more likely to be premature or have low birth weight; mother has higher risk of complications; this is why only one or two embryos are inserted.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): clear explanation of how both fertility drugs and IVF can cause multiple births, with risks to mother and babies.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple statements, e.g. more than one embryo inserted, or twins are risky.
0 marks: no relevant content.
questions.explanation: Cover both causes (several eggs released, more than one embryo inserted) and both groups at risk (babies and mother).

questions.question: Describe the steps of IVF treatment and explain the role of hormones in it.
markScheme: Indicative content: the mother is given FSH and LH; FSH stimulates the maturation of several eggs; LH helps final maturation and release, allowing eggs to be collected at the right time; eggs are collected from the mother's ovaries; eggs are fertilised by sperm from the father in the laboratory; fertilised eggs develop into embryos; embryos are checked under a microscope; at the stage when they are tiny balls of cells, one or two embryos are inserted into the mother's uterus; an embryo must implant in the uterus lining; pregnancy then continues as normal.
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): all main steps in the correct order with a clear explanation of why FSH and LH are given.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): most steps in order, with some reference to hormones.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): one or two steps or hormones named with little sequence.
0 marks: no relevant content.
questions.explanation: Sequence matters in 'describe the steps'. Explaining that FSH makes SEVERAL eggs mature is the key point for the hormone part.

questions.question: Evaluate the use of IVF to treat infertility, from the points of view of both the patients and the doctors.
markScheme: Indicative content, benefits: gives a woman the chance to have a baby of her own; can help when oviducts are blocked or other treatments have failed; embryos can be checked before insertion; spare embryos can be frozen for later attempts.

Drawbacks for patients: very emotionally and physically stressful; injections and egg collection procedures; success rates are not high, especially in older women; may need several expensive cycles; risk of multiple births.

Doctors' perspective: must consider the health and safety of mother and babies; limit embryos to one or two to reduce multiple births; success rates and use of resources; ethical issues about unused embryos.
Conclusion: a justified judgement, e.g. IVF is worthwhile for many couples who cannot otherwise conceive, provided risks are reduced and couples are supported.
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): balanced evaluation including both patient and doctor perspectives, with a justified conclusion.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): some benefits and drawbacks, perhaps from one perspective only; conclusion may be missing.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple statements of benefits or drawbacks.
0 marks: no relevant content.
questions.explanation: Make sure you address both perspectives named in the question, use the specification's three drawbacks, and finish with a reasoned conclusion.
